core_obligations: Produce a minimal element of the set of closed subschemes on which P holds (proof lines 17066-17068): let T be the set of closed subschemes T' of T with P(T'); by hypothesis (2) this set has a minimal element T'.

Show that the minimal T' is reduced (proof line 17068): by hypothesis (1), thickening-invariance, a non-reduced T' could be replaced by its reduced subscheme with the same underlying space, contradicting minimality.

Pass to the generic point of an irreducible component (proof lines 17069-17074): pick eta in T' the generic point of an irreducible component, write eta = Spec(K) and eta = lim V over the affine open subschemes V of T' containing eta, then use hypothesis (3) and minimality of T' to get P(V) for all those V.
Conclude P(eta) (proof lines 17074-17075): apply hypothesis (2) to the inverse system of the V to obtain P(eta), which is the required after-fact P(Spec(K)) for the morphism Spec(K) -> T.
proof_roadmap: Take the set of closed subschemes of T satisfying P and use the limit hypothesis to find a minimal one.
Take the generic point eta of an irreducible component; it is Spec(K) for a field K and a limit of the affine open subschemes V containing it.
Hypothesis (3) plus minimality gives P(V) for all such V, and the limit hypothesis then gives P(eta).
difficulty_reason: The lemma is a deformation-and-limit argument: a property P of quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes over T that is thickening-invariant, stable under limits along affine transition maps, and decomposable along a closed subscheme with quasi-compact complement must hold at some field-valued point of T (statement lines 17045-17063). The proof chooses a minimal closed subscheme T' satisfying P (proof lines 17066-17068), uses thickening-invariance to see that T' is reduced, then takes the generic point eta of an irreducible component and realises it both as Spec(K) and as the limit of the affine open subschemes V containing it (proof lines 17069-17072); the decomposition hypothesis and minimality then give P(V) and hypothesis (2) upgrades this to P(eta) (proof lines 17073-17075). Each of the three hypotheses is used exactly once and in a different place, which is the non-formal content. The claim is H2: a short but genuinely three-step descent, all inside the counted span.
